# Deckers Outdoor (DECK) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator's note: transcripts span FY25 Q4 (2025-05-22) through FY26 Q4 (2026-05-21) — six consecutive quarterly calls plus the FY25 year-end anchor. Management voices: Stefano Caroti (CEO, first full year as president/CEO across this window) and Steve Fasching (CFO). The forensic test below cross-references every load-bearing claim against the screener's actual multi-year financials.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across these six quarters is a controlled, almost monotonous narrative of "two best-in-class brands compounding through a hostile macro" — and the remarkable thing is how little the script changed even as the numbers cooled. Three arcs run through it:

**(a) From "16% revenue / 30% EPS" euphoria to "double-digit is the new normal."** The FY25 year-end call (2025-05-22) opened from a position of peak strength: "revenue growing 16% versus last year, to just shy of $5 billion… earnings per share increasing 30%." By the FY26 year-end call (2026-05-21) the headline had compressed to "total Deckers revenue increased 10%… record earnings per share to $7.02, reflecting an 11% increase." Management never frames this as deceleration — it is always reframed as "another record year." The growth *rate* halved (EPS +30% → +11%) while the *language* stayed at full conviction. That gap is the single most important feature of this dossier.

**(b) The deliberate channel pivot: DTC → wholesale.** At the start of the window (FY25 Q4 and FY26 Q1) management was visibly defensive about HOKA DTC weakness — "ongoing pressure in the U.S. online channel" (FY26 Q1) — and leaned into a *new* framing that wholesale strength is a *feature*, not a bug: "consumers often search for deals online, but brick-and-mortar stores remain the primary venue for full price sales" (FY26 Q1). This was repeated almost verbatim every quarter. By FY26 Q3 (2026-01-29) they declared the inflection won: HOKA US "positively inflecting." This is a genuine thesis pivot dressed as continuity — the 50/50 DTC/wholesale "long-term aim" was used to retroactively justify what was actually a near-term DTC stumble.

**(c) Tariffs introduced (FY26 Q1), escalated (Q2-Q3), then partially neutralized (Q4).** Trade policy appears in FY25 Q4 as "significant uncertainty," forces the company to *withhold full-year FY26 guidance* (FY26 Q1), drives the explicit margin-pressure guide ("the change you're seeing in the back half is tariff-driven," FY26 Q2), and by FY26 Q4 resolves into a quantified, bounded number: "the gross amount we paid was around $120 million" under IEEPA, now subject to refund. The tariff arc is the cleanest example of management's pattern: name the risk early, bound it, then absorb it without breaking the margin story.

Growth drivers *introduced*: HOKA lifestyle extension (Mafate family, lower-profile shoes), HOKA membership program (credited for the Q3 DTC inflection), international as the load-bearing engine. Drivers *quietly dropped*: the Koolaburra brand (phased out — used in Q3 to explain a segment revenue *decline*), and the early-window emphasis on aggressive DTC retail store expansion (repeatedly walked back to "we have a much smaller retail footprint").

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Mgmt claim (quarter) | The actual financials | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "another record year… record EPS $7.02" (FY26 Q4) | EPS trajectory 2.71→3.23→4.86→6.33→7.02; rev 3.15B→3.63B→4.29B→4.99B→5.45B | **TRUE but decelerating.** Record is real; but EPS growth collapsed from +30.5% (FY25) to +10.9% (FY26), and rev growth from +16% to +9.4%. |
| "best-in-class operating margins above 23%" (FY26 Q4) | Gross 56.1% (stable), net 18.8%, FCF margin 20.1%, ROE 34.8%, ROIC 28.3% | **TRUE and corroborated.** This is the strongest, most defensible claim. ROIC 28.3% is genuinely best-in-footwear (peers: CROX 18.7%, SKX ~12%, ONON ~8%). |
| "fortified balance sheet… share repurchase program" (FY26 Q3/Q4) | Net CASH $1.53B (cash $1.91B vs total debt $375M), Altman-Z 12.0 | **TRUE and load-bearing.** The balance sheet is a fortress; $5B total buyback authorization (~28% of a ~$17–18B cap) is the real forcing function. |
| "consumer is still showing up for our brand" / demand "incredibly strong" (every quarter) | Rev +9.4% YoY, but *latest-Q EPS YoY −3%* (TTM block); HOKA Q1-FY27 guided to *high-single-digit* | **PARTIALLY DIVERGENT.** Demand is real but cooling; the −3% latest-Q EPS and HSD HOKA guide contradict the unbroken "incredibly strong" framing. |
| "we manage a scarcity model… high levels of gross margin" (FY25 Q4) | Gross margin 56.1% flagged as 0.93σ *below* historic peak | **TRUE but at/near peak.** Scarcity model is real, but margins are described as 0.93σ from peak — limited expansion runway; FY27 guide embeds *more promotion + tariff/input-cost pressure*. |
| Beat "7/7 quarters (100%)" implied by tone | Screener confirms beat 7/7 qtrs | **TRUE.** Genuine sandbagging/beat culture (see §4). |

The "billions of runway" claim is aspirational, not yet in the numbers. |

**Net forensic read:** The financials *support* the quality, balance-sheet, and returns claims unambiguously — there is no accounting smell, no working-capital game, no channel-stuffing tell (inventory is *down*, full-price selling *up*). Where the narrative outruns the numbers is exclusively on **growth durability**: management speaks at FY25's +30% conviction level while delivering FY26's +11%. The story is richer than the trajectory on growth, and exactly as good as the trajectory on quality.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: STABLE-to-modestly-rising in tone, even as fundamentals decelerated — a confidence/reality gap.**

- **FY25 Q4 (2025-05-22):** Offensive, victory-lap. "exceptional year… record performance." But the *first* defensive note appears: "significant amount of uncertainty introduced as a result of shifting US trade policy."
- **FY26 Q1 (2025-07-24):** Defensive undertone surfaces. "navigating a choppy U.S. consumer environment"; DTC "ongoing pressure in the U.S. online channel." Withholds FY26 guidance. This is the low point of confidence.
- **FY26 Q2 (2025-10-23):** Stabilizing. "outstanding second-quarter results ahead of our expectations." But explicit margin warning: tariff pressure "will continue into FY '27."
- **FY26 Q3 (2026-01-29):** Confidence re-rising. "outstanding third quarter… positive inflection" in US; "this increases our optimism going into next year." The membership-program win is the proof point they lean on.
- **FY26 Q4 (2026-05-21):** Back to full offense. "exceptional results, strong momentum and deep conviction in the durability of our model"; unveils a *multi-year 2030 framework* (HSD revenue / LDD EPS) — a confidence signal, committing to multi-year targets they previously refused to give.

**Shift pattern:** The window runs offensive → defensive (Q1 trough) → re-offensive, tracking the US-consumer scare and its resolution. Crucially, by Q4 management moved *from refusing FY26 guidance to issuing a 4-year framework* — the single clearest "confidence restored" tell. Guidance specificity *increased* over the window. No shift to pure cost/efficiency language; investment in brand-building was reaffirmed every quarter ("oversized investments in the brand").

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: HIGH.**

- The screener confirms a **7/7 quarter beat rate (100%)** — and the transcripts show the *mechanism*: a deliberate scarcity/sandbag model. CFO Fasching, FY26 Q2: "Our assumption always embeds a level of more normalized promotion, and then we'll see how things play out. And if they play out like Q1, we may see some upside." That is textbook conservative-guide language, and the 7/7 beat confirms it works.
- **Tariff guide tracked honestly:** they pre-warned back-half FY26 margin pressure (Q2), then delivered it without a negative surprise, and quantified the $120M IEEPA cash cost (Q4). No goalpost-moving.
- **HOKA guide reset transparently:** "pre-tariff environment, we saw mid-teens… now with a tariff imposed world in the back half, we're low teens" (FY26 Q2). They told analysts the math and then beat the lowered bar (HOKA +18% in Q3).
- **The one credibility caveat:** the FY27 guide embeds HOKA decelerating to *high-single-digit in the June quarter* and *low-double-digit for the year* — the first time the headline HOKA number drops below mid-teens. Given the 100% beat history this is likely sandbagged, but it is also the first guide that *admits* deceleration. Credibility of the *numbers* is high; the open question is whether the sandbag cushion shrinks as growth matures.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **HOKA US DTC weakness — the dominant recurring pressure.** Sam Poser (Williams Trading) hammered this every call, pushing for store-vs-ecommerce comp specifics: "To what degree… 150 basis points. Can you please give us something here?" (FY26 Q1). Management *repeatedly declined to break it out*: "I don't know, Sam, that we want to go down a path of breaking out that level of detail." This is the clearest sustained non-answer in the transcripts — a deflection on the exact metric (US DTC comp) that was the soft spot.
- **Margin durability / tariff permanence.** Jonathan Komp (Baird, FY26 Q2): "is that more temporary? Or is that a permanent step down in the margin?" Management's answer was a qualified "headwinds in the back half that will continue into FY '27" — an admission that the margin hit is *not* fully transitory, only that it is tariff-driven rather than demand-driven.
- **HOKA deceleration framing.** Jay Sole (UBS, FY26 Q2) pressed on whether FY25 was a "transition year." CEO conceded directly: "yes, it's a bit of a transition year. We probably have masked a few too many big product launches in the first half… it was a learning year for us." A rare, credible admission of self-inflicted execution error.
- **What analysts worry about that management under-addresses:** the *durability* of the wholesale-led growth model. Management frames the DTC→wholesale shift as strategic, but the channel mix shift mechanically pressures gross margin (wholesale carries lower margin than DTC), and the "50/50 long-term aim" conveniently caps how much they have to defend DTC softness. No analyst fully cornered them on the margin math of a structurally more-wholesale mix.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **EPS growth more than halved** — +30.5% (FY25) → +10.9% (FY26) — while management language stayed at peak conviction. The narrative-reality gap is the core risk.

# Deckers Outdoor (DECK) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator dossier · 6 consecutive earnings calls FY25-Q4 (2025-05-22) → FY26-Q4 (2026-05-21) · cross-referenced against the screener's hard financials. Allocating real capital.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across these six calls is remarkably **consistent in structure but quietly contracting in growth rate** — a maturing two-brand compounder learning to operate in a tariff-and-weak-US-consumer regime.

- **FY25-Q4 (May-2025) — peak triumphalism.** The opening call is a victory lap: FY25 revenue "just shy of $5 billion" +16%, gross margin 57.9% (+230bp), operating margin 23.6%, EPS $6.33 +30%. Management frames a five-year record: 19% revenue CAGR, HOKA +$1.9B, UGG +$1.0B, 32% EPS CAGR. The forward-looking note that dates the whole series appears here: "a significant amount of uncertainty introduced as a result of shifting US trade policy." They decline to guide the full year and lean on the "50/50 DTC/wholesale" target and "scarcity model" as the margin-defense framework.
- **FY26-Q1 (Jul-2025) — the wobble.** Revenue +17% to $965M, EPS $0.93 +24% — but the texture turns defensive: **US revenue DOWN 3%**, international +50%, HOKA US DTC pressured, and management openly admits "execution challenges we faced over the last six months" and "adjusting product life cycles." The narrative pivots from "best year ever" to "navigating a choppy US consumer environment." The new load-bearing claim — *international is the engine, US is the problem child* — is introduced here and persists.
- **FY26-Q2 (Oct-2025) — stabilization, margin warning.** Revenue +9%, EPS +14%; H1 total +12%, HOKA +15%, UGG +12%. Management starts pre-announcing **back-half margin compression "driven by the tariffs"** that "will continue into FY '27." This is the first explicit forward margin-down flag, and it is honest.
- **FY26-Q3 (Jan-2026) — the inflection.** The best call of the set: revenue +7% to $1.96B, record EPS $3.33 +11%, and critically **US "positive inflection" +5%** after two soft quarters, HOKA +18%, UGG +5%, full-price selling preserved. Management's tone visibly relaxes ("the brands did show up, and this increases our optimism"). Koolaburra phase-out introduced as the explanation for optical segment declines.
- **FY26-Q4 (May-2026) — record close + first multi-year framework.** FY26 revenue ~$5.47B +10%, EPS $7.02 +11%, OM "above 23%", HOKA $2.587B +16%, UGG $2.739B +8%. The genuinely NEW disclosure is a **2028-2030 framework: "low double-digit EPS growth"** and HOKA "low double-digit" with a $100B-category TAM claim. They quantify tariffs paid (~$120M under IEEPA) and flag a refund that is filed but NOT in guidance.

**Growth drivers introduced/dropped:** HOKA "experience centers" / flagship retail (FY25-Q4) faded to a minor note. The persistent, strengthening driver is **wholesale-door expansion + international awareness (HOKA US 50→60%, Europe 30→40%, China →30%)**. The persistent risk-driver is the **US consumer + tariffs**. The story did not shift category — it decelerated from "+16-19% hypergrowth" to a self-described "+10% / low-double-digit" maturity.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Mgmt claim | Quarter | Hard financials say | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Record performance… revenue grew 16%" | FY25-Q4 | FY25 rev 4.99B vs 4.29B = +16.3% ✓; NI 760→966M | **Corroborated** |

**Where the story is RICHER than the numbers:** the "$100B / $0.5T TAM, billions of runway" HOKA framing (FY26-Q2/Q4) is aspirational against a base now growing low-double-digit with **decelerating** YoY (FY26-Q3 +7%, latest-Q EPS -3% YoY). ---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable-to-Rising (dipped mid-series, recovered).** A clean U-shape.

- **FY25-Q4 — high/offensive:** "another exceptional year… winning strategy… bright future ahead."
- **FY26-Q1 — defensive/cautious:** "choppy US consumer," "execution challenges we faced over the last six months," "we will continue to feel some pressure." Most defensive call of the set.
- **FY26-Q2 — guarded:** margin warnings, "we'll see how the consumer shows up… we're better positioned than most."
- **FY26-Q3 — confidence restored:** "we've been cautious about the economy and the consumer, but never about our brands… the brands did show up, and this increases our optimism."
- **FY26-Q4 — confident, forward-leaning:** "deep conviction in the durability of our model," and they put a **2028-2030 numeric framework** on the table — a signal of confidence, since maturing companies only volunteer multi-year targets when they believe them.

Specificity with guidance **increased** over time (from "won't guide the full year" in FY25-Q4 to an explicit FY27 + multi-year framework by FY26-Q4). The offense→defense→offense rotation tracks the US-consumer arc, not a structural loss of nerve.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: HIGH.**

- Screener: **beat 7/7 quarters (100%).** This is corroborated by the narrative — every call references results "ahead of expectations."
- The cleanest closed loop: in FY26-Q2 management guided HOKA "low teens with tariffs" (vs pre-tariff mid-teens) and flagged back-half margin pressure; by FY26-Q4 HOKA delivered +16% for the year and margins held above 23% despite tariffs — they **over-delivered on a conservatively-set bar.**
- FY26-Q2's explicit "margin pressure will continue into FY '27" was honored — FY27 guide is GM 56.5% (down from 57.7%), OM ~21.5% — so they did not bury the bad news.
- **Sandbagging pattern: YES, mild and constructive.** The "scarcity model… we run lean on inventory" framing (FY25-Q4, FY26-Q4) is a deliberate under-ship-to-protect-margin posture that structurally seeds beats. This is high-quality sandbagging (protects gross margin and pull-forward demand), not number-gaming.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **US DTC comp granularity (Sam Poser, repeatedly).** In FY26-Q1, Poser pushed hard for the stores-vs-ecommerce split ("Can you please give us something here? I really think it's important") and management **refused to break it out** ("I don't know, Sam, that we want to go down a path of breaking out that level of detail"). A persistent transparency gap on the channel that was the actual weak point.
- **Margin durability (Komp/Sole, FY26-Q2).** Analysts pressed whether the back-half margin step-down was temporary (tariff) or permanent. Management attributed it cleanly to tariffs and promised FY27 first-half pressure — this one did NOT turn into a worse-than-said surprise; it was handled straight.
- **HOKA US DTC inflection durability (Rick Patel, FY26-Q3/Q4).** Analysts repeatedly probed whether the Q3 US inflection was real or timing. Management credited the membership program + cleaner marketplace — and Q4 confirmed continued US positivity, so the worry resolved favorably.
- **The unresolved worry analysts keep circling:** is HOKA's growth structurally decelerating (the "transition year," product-cadence missteps) or just digesting? Management's answer — "$100B TAM, plenty of upside" — is a deflection-by-TAM rather than a unit-economics answer.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Growth deceleration is real and visible:** revenue YoY cooled from +16% (FY25) to +10% (FY26); **latest-Q EPS YoY -3%**; FY27 guide is only +4-6% EPS. The compounding rate has stepped down.
🔴 **Gross margin has PEAKED** (0.93σ vs historical peak; FY27 guided DOWN to 56.5% from 57.7%) — tariffs + input inflation are a real, persisting headwind into FY27 H1.
🔴 **US consumer remains soft / event-driven**; growth is carried by international, exposing the thesis to FX and a single-region engine.
🔴 **Channel-transparency gap** — management refused repeated requests to disaggregate US DTC.
🔴 **Two-brand concentration** — UGG (50%) + HOKA (47%) = 97% of revenue; HOKA is fashion-cycle-exposed performance footwear in a category (CROX, ONON, NKE, SKX) where brand heat can cool fast.

🟢 **Fortress balance sheet:** NET CASH $1.53B, ROE 34.8%, ROIC 28.3% — among the best in footwear.
🟢 **100% beat rate (7/7)** with a credible, mildly-sandbagged guidance posture.
🟢 **Aggressive, accretive buyback** at a de-rated price: authorization lifted to **$8.05B** (~30%+ of a ~$16-17B market cap), $1.075B repurchased in FY26 — the dominant capital-return forcing function.
🟢 **International runway genuinely early** (HOKA Europe 40%, China 30% awareness vs US 60%) — a real multi-year volume lever, independently confirmed by +38-50% international growth.
🟢 **Pricing power intact** — "we haven't seen any material decline… after we raised prices" (FY26-Q1), full-price selling preserved through a weak US tape.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **Terminology shift toward "franchises as platforms / product families"** (FY26-Q2→Q4): "Our franchises function as scalable platforms representing families of products, rather than single styles." This is management re-coding HOKA from a hit-driven shoe business toward a more durable, platform-extension narrative — partly to pre-empt the "what happens when Bondi/Clifton cools" question.
- **The "scarcity model" is doing heavy lifting** as the margin-defense story. It is genuinely effective (drives full-price selling + reorders) but it also CAPS the achievable growth rate — you cannot scarcity-model your way to 20% growth. Management has implicitly chosen margin/brand-equity over volume, which is the right long-term call but explains the deceleration.
- **Tariff accounting tell (FY26-Q4):** ~$120M IEEPA paid, refund filed but explicitly excluded from guidance, with "partners who were cost-sharing" — meaning any refund is partly owed back to wholesale partners. The refund is a **diluted, uncertain-timing option, not a clean per-share windfall.**
- **Multi-year framework as a maturity signal:** volunteering 2028-2030 "low-double-digit EPS" is the language of a company transitioning from growth story to **compounder** — and it is being priced as such (P/FCF 14x, not 40x).
- CEO Stefano Caroti (relatively new in the seat across this series) is consistent and operationally fluent; no management-instability tell.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE** (high-quality compounder, decelerating but not deteriorating; capital allocation is a clear positive).

The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing: **this is a quality-at-a-fair-price deep-value name, NOT a catalyst special-sit.** The thesis is "a 28% ROIC, net-cash, 100%-beat compounder is trading at ~14x P/FCF — roughly half the multiple of ONON/BIRK and a fraction of its own history — because growth decelerated to ~10% and margins guided down on tariffs." The re-rate from the record FY26 is largely **spent** (stock ~$110, near consensus), and FY27 is a **margin-DOWN year**, so the catalyst is structural (relentless buyback + international volume + eventual tariff normalization), not a dated event. The honest read: **NARROW moat (footwear/fashion is inherently cyclical and brand-heat-dependent) that is currently STABLE at peak returns.** The terminal risk is not secular displacement but **fashion-cycle cooling of HOKA** — a cyclical/idiosyncratic risk, not a structural one.

The genuine risk to terminal value is mono-brand fashion risk (HOKA heat fading), which is cyclical and manageable given UGG's 40-year durability and the net-cash balance sheet.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

By the July 2025 call (first quarter of fiscal 2026), a new and honest theme entered: tariffs and a "choppy U.S. consumer." Management began separating two worlds — a still-booming international business (up ~38-50% across the first half) and a pressured U.S. consumer. A second new theme was the deliberate lean into wholesale doors for HOKA, framed not as a strategy change but as "taking advantage of the opportunity" of rising brand awareness; they were candid this would pressure direct-to-consumer growth near term. By the January 2026 call (third quarter), the U.S. had "positively inflected" and the membership program was credited for repeat-purchase strength. The May 2026 year-end call closed fiscal 2026 with record revenue of nearly $5.5 billion and introduced a forward "multiyear framework" out to fiscal 2030 (low-double-digit EPS growth) — a shift from "prove HOKA can grow" to "here is the durable long-range model."

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| "Industry-leading profitability… operating margins above 23%" | Gross margin 56.1% (stable, near historical peak), net margin 18.8%, free-cash-flow margin ~20%. | Matches — genuinely best-in-class for footwear. |
| "Record EPS of $7.02, up 11%" | EPS 7.02 vs 6.33 (+10.9%); trailing-twelve-month diluted EPS 7.03. | Matches exactly. |
| "Fortified balance sheet… share repurchases" | Net cash of $1.53B (cash 1.91B vs total debt 375M). Fresh $3.5B buyback authorized (May 2026). | Matches and then some — a fortress. |

bull_thesis: The bull case is that the market has applied a broken-footwear-brand multiple to a business that is not broken. At $99.23 Deckers trades at about 14 times trailing earnings and roughly 13 times the midpoint of its own guidance, on an enterprise value (market value plus debt, less cash) of about $12.7 billion against trailing free cash flow of $1.18 billion -- a free-cash-flow yield near 8.6%, with genuine net cash of $1.13 billion behind it. The quality that multiple is being applied to is exceptional and verifiable: return on invested capital of 28.3%, return on equity of 34.8%, no goodwill on the balance sheet, no long-term borrowings, a Piotroski financial-health score of 7 of 9, and twelve consecutive quarters of beating consensus earnings. The load-bearing evidence for durability is the gross margin. Deckers absorbed an import tax, raised prices, and its gross margin went UP -- 56.4% in the June 2026 quarter against 55.8% a year earlier, with fiscal 2027 guided above 56.5%, higher than the year just completed. Management's claim in January 2026 that 'the quarter demonstrates that we have more pricing power' is the rare boast the numbers actually corroborate, and its July 2025 observation that after price rises 'we haven't seen any material decline in performance' is the mechanism. Three things then have to hold for the bull case. One, HOKA's international runway converts: brand awareness is 60% in the US but only 40% in Europe and 30% in China, US sporting-goods distribution is 50% penetrated and run-specialty only 25%, and in Europe those figures are 40% and under 20%. That is the arithmetic behind the low-double-digit growth framework management committed to for fiscal 2028 through 2030 -- the first multi-year commitment it has made in this window, and it was made while guiding a down-margin year. Two, the roughly 21.5% operating margin guided for fiscal 2027 proves to be a trough rather than a plateau. The case that it is a trough is straightforward: the decline is not a pricing failure, since gross margin is rising, but a deliberate marketing and international-infrastructure step-up plus a tariff, and management pre-warned in October 2025 that the pressure was a fiscal 2027 first-half event. Three, and least appreciated, the buyback keeps running. The company retired $338.2 million of stock in one quarter at roughly $102 a share and has about $4.7 billion still authorised -- roughly a third of the company. At that pace the share count shrinks 9-10% a year, self-funded, which adds several points annually to earnings per share that consensus does not fully carry, and requires no activist and no corporate event to happen. Two free options sit on top: roughly $120 million of tariff paid under the emergency-powers regime is refundable and is explicitly excluded from guidance ('this outlook does not assume the collection of refunds for tariffs previously paid'), and the 12.5% tariff rate baked into the plan reflects a proposed, not final, trade measure that could settle lower.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that this is a good business at a fair price whose earnings are near a cyclical peak, and that the cheapness is arithmetic rather than opportunity. Start with the deceleration, which is not subtle. HOKA grew 24% in fiscal 2025, 16% in fiscal 2026, and 7.7% in the June 2026 quarter -- the growth rate has more than halved in two years, against a stated plan of low-double-digit growth through fiscal 2030 that now requires a re-acceleration nobody has explained. UGG grew 4.9% in the same quarter. Company revenue growth of 5.7% is a mid-single-digit business, and guided earnings per share of $7.35-7.50 against $7.02 delivered is 5-7% growth, not the 27% five-year compound rate that built the reputation. A 14-times multiple on a 6%-grower is not obviously cheap. Second, the margin question cuts the wrong way. Operating margin was 23.6% in fiscal 2025, above 23% in fiscal 2026, and is guided to roughly 21.5% for fiscal 2027 -- two consecutive years of decline -- and the screener flags current margins at 0.93 standard deviations above their own historical peak. In the June 2026 quarter operating expenses grew 12.7% against 5.7% revenue growth, taking operating margin down about two points to 15.2% and leaving earnings per share flat at $0.94 versus $0.93. Management has never bridged that spending, never quantified a return on it, and never named the year it normalises. If margin settles at 18% rather than 21.5% -- still an excellent number, and roughly where it sat in fiscal 2023 -- the same multiple puts the shares near where they trade today and the discount vanishes entirely. Third, the sandbag is thinning. The company beat consensus by roughly 36% in the June 2025 quarter, then 15%, 20%, 18%, and only 6.8% in June 2026. The reflex that Deckers always beats big is now a materially weaker plank than it was a year ago. Fourth, footwear brands are mortal in a way that balance sheets do not protect against. HOKA is a 17-year-old performance-running label competing with On Holding, Brooks, Asics, New Balance and a recovering Nike; UGG is a fashion franchise at a record high. The market has watched Crocs, Skechers, Under Armour and Nike itself de-rate hard once growth stalled, and it is pricing Deckers for the same arc -- which is a rational prior, not an error. Fifth, the near-term setting is hostile: this is a discretionary consumer brand with roughly half its business in a soft US market, into a second oil shock with Brent around $89-100, and the assumed 12.5% tariff rate is not final and could go higher. Insiders are not buying -- one open-market purchase of 1,825 shares against fourteen sales totalling 17,396. What would confirm the bear case: gross margin slipping below about 55% alongside rising promotional activity, HOKA US growth turning negative, or operating expenses continuing to compound at more than twice revenue into fiscal 2028.
consensus_delta: For a business the screener flags as deep value, the right question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable or growing earning power. Here it is pricing something subtler and mostly defensible -- so our disagreement with the street is real but narrow, and we say so plainly rather than manufacture an edge. The street's central assumption, visible in the 24 July target cuts, is that fiscal 2027's roughly 21.5% operating margin marks a step down to a new plateau rather than a trough. We think that assumption is being made on the wrong evidence. Analysts are reading the two-point operating-margin decline in the June quarter as competitive pressure, when the gross margin -- the only line that actually measures pricing power -- went the OTHER way, rising to 56.4% from 55.8% while the company absorbed an import tax and raised prices. The entire decline sits in operating expenses, which grew 12.7% against 5.7% revenue growth. That is a spending decision, and the company guided fiscal 2027 gross margin ABOVE the year just completed. A business losing pricing power cannot do that. Where we genuinely disagree in a way that is worth money: first, the buyback. Deckers retired $338.2 million of stock in a single quarter and has about $4.7 billion authorised, roughly a third of the company; at that pace the share count falls 9-10% a year, self-funded from cash flow. Consensus models nothing like that rate, and it adds several points a year to earnings per share without any operating improvement at all. Second, the tariff assumption. The plan now embeds 12.5%, raised from 10%, against a replacement trade measure that is proposed and not final -- and this management has beaten its own guidance in twelve consecutive quarters. A lower final rate makes the guide conservative twice over. Where the street is right and we will not argue: HOKA's growth really has fallen from 24% to 16% to 7.7% in two years, and a 14-times multiple on a mid-single-digit grower is not an anomaly. The decisive discipline is this -- our own $118 base case lands essentially on the street's post-cut consensus of about $118. When our estimate of worth equals the sell-side's, we do not have an expectations arbitrage; we have agreement at a modest discount. That is worth a watchlist, not a position.

The dated events, in order. The September-quarter report on 22 October 2026 is the first hard date and the most important one, because management has already guided it below street expectations and because it is the first quarter in which the inventory-timing mitigations that protected earlier periods are exhausted. Consensus sits at $1.80 of earnings per share on $1.51 billion of revenue. A print that holds gross margin above 56% while operating-expense growth decelerates toward revenue growth would settle the trough-versus-plateau question in the bulls' favour and is the cleanest single catalyst available. The January 2027 report is the confirmation, and the fiscal 2028 guidance that arrives with the fourth-quarter report in May 2027 is where the multi-year framework -- HOKA growing low double digits from fiscal 2028 through 2030 -- either gets underwritten or gets abandoned. That May 2027 date is the real one for the full base case, which is why we set an 18-month horizon. Two undated but live items sit alongside: the finalisation of the replacement US trade measure, which determines whether the 12.5% tariff assumption in the plan proves conservative or optimistic, and the collection of roughly $120 million of previously paid tariff that is explicitly excluded from guidance -- modest in size, partly owed onward to wholesale partners, and undated, so we credit it only in the favourable case. And then the mechanism that requires no event at all, which for a deep-value name is the most reliable forcing function of the three types the framework looks for: the company is buying back 9-10% of its own shares a year out of cash flow, with roughly a third of the company still authorised. No activist is needed, no asset sale, no strategic review. If the operating business merely holds flat, the per-share numbers rise anyway. The two quarters to be reported in October 2026 and January 2027 are where the market decides whether 21.5% is a trough or a plateau, and that is the whole valuation. Third, the macro overlay, which is genuinely adverse right now. This is a discretionary consumer brand with roughly half its revenue in a US market management has described as under pressure for four consecutive calls, heading into a second oil shock with Brent in the high $80s to above $100 and consumer sentiment already weak. Layered on that, the replacement trade measure behind the 12.5% assumption is not final and could settle higher, and the current tape is punishing exactly this profile -- companies that raise guidance but spend more, which have been marked down hard across this earnings season. # Deckers Brands (DECK) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Forensic review of six consecutive quarterly earnings calls, May 2025 through July 2026, cross-checked against the reported financials. Share price used throughout: $99.23 (New York listing, US dollars, 27 July 2026).*

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Deckers sells two footwear brands: UGG, the 45-year-old sheepskin-boot franchise that has become a year-round premium lifestyle label, and HOKA, the thick-soled running brand it bought in 2013 and has grown into a roughly $2.9 billion business. A handful of small brands (Teva, AHNU, and the now-discontinued Koolaburra) make up the remaining 2-3% of sales.

Across these six calls the story moves through three distinct phases, and the shift is unusually easy to date.

**Phase one — victory lap (May 2025).** The fiscal 2025 wrap-up is the most confident management has sounded in the entire window. Revenue grew 16% to just under $5 billion, gross margin expanded 230 basis points to 57.9%, operating margin rose 200 basis points to 23.6%, and earnings per share grew 30% to $6.33. Chief executive Stefano Caroti framed it against a five-year record: revenue compounding at 19% a year, HOKA adding about $1.9 billion of revenue, UGG adding $1 billion, and earnings per share compounding at 32%. The word that recurs is "exceptional."

**Phase two — the tariff siege (July 2025 through January 2026).** Almost immediately the frame narrows. On the May 2025 call Caroti already flagged "a significant amount of uncertainty introduced as a result of shifting US trade policy," and for the next three quarters the story becomes a two-track narrative: brands winning, margins under a policy tax. By October 2025, chief financial officer Steve Fasching is explicit that the back-half margin decline is "really being driven by the tariffs," and — importantly — that the pressure "will continue into FY '27." The HOKA growth plan was cut from mid-teens (set before tariffs) to low teens (with them). Management is careful, repeatedly, to separate the two: demand is not the problem, the import tax is.

**Phase three — the brands answer, then the cost line bites (January 2026 through July 2026).** The January 2026 quarter is the vindication. Record revenue of $1.96 billion, HOKA up 18%, US revenue inflecting positively after two soft quarters, record earnings per share of $3.33, and this line from Fasching: "the quarter demonstrates that we have more pricing power." Caroti's summary is the most quotable thing in the transcripts: "We've been cautious about the economy and the consumer, but never about our brands."

The most recent quarter (reported 23 July 2026, after the transcript set) is where the arc turns again — and this time the pressure is self-inflicted rather than imposed. Revenue crossed $1 billion in a June quarter for the first time, up 5.7%. Gross margin actually *rose*, to 56.4% from 55.8%. But operating expenses grew 12.7% against 5.7% revenue growth, and earnings per share came in at $0.94 versus $0.93 a year earlier — essentially flat. The growth driver that was quietly retired over this window is US demand; the one that replaced it is international, which grew 50% in the June 2025 quarter and 38% across the first half of fiscal 2026.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

Management's biggest claims, tested against what the numbers actually did.

| Management's claim | Where and when | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pricing power is real; price rises stick | "we haven't seen any material decline in performance for the products that we have raised price on" (Jul 2025); "we have more pricing power" (Jan 2026) | Gross margin held 56-58% straight through a tariff shock, and in the June 2026 quarter *rose* to 56.4% from 55.8%. Fiscal 2027 gross margin is guided "slightly better than 56.5%" — above the year just finished | **Supported.** This is the single best-evidenced claim in the file |
| The scarcity model protects margin | "we manage a scarcity model. When we run low, it's helping us maintain high levels of gross margin" (May 2025) | Inventory at 31 March 2026 was down low single digits year on year while revenue grew 10%; gross margin stayed above 56% | **Supported** |
| Margin pressure is tariffs, not the business | "the declines that we're reflecting are really being driven by the tariffs" (Oct 2025) | Only partly true now. In the June 2026 quarter gross margin *improved* 60 basis points, yet operating margin fell roughly 200 basis points to 15.2%. The entire decline came from operating expenses of $419.9 million, up 12.7%. That is a spending decision, not an import tax | **Diverges.** The narrative under-owns a deliberate cost step-up |
| International is the growth engine | Emphasised every quarter from Jul 2025 | International revenue +50% (Jun 2025 quarter), +38% (first half fiscal 2026), +15% (Dec 2025 quarter). HOKA brand awareness US 60%, Europe 40%, China 30% (May 2026) | **Supported**, though the growth rate is decelerating sharply quarter by quarter |
| HOKA is gaining share | "HOKA gained 2 points of market share in the overall US Road running category" (Oct 2025, citing Circana) | HOKA grew 24% (fiscal 2025), 16% (fiscal 2026), and 7.7% in the June 2026 quarter. Share gains are real; the growth rate has more than halved in two years | **Supported but decaying** |
| Returns and balance sheet strength | Referenced via "fortified balance sheet" (Jan 2026) | Return on invested capital 28.3%, return on equity 34.8%, and genuine net cash of $1.13 billion at 30 June 2026 (cash of $1.60 billion against total debt of $472 million including $399 million of capitalised leases). No goodwill on the balance sheet | **Supported, and understated by management** |

**Where the story is richer than the numbers justify:** the framing of margin pressure as externally imposed. Three consecutive calls trained investors to read margin decline as a tariff story. The June 2026 quarter shows the gross margin — the true measure of pricing power — going the *right* way while operating margin falls two full points on internal spending. That is a materially different problem, and management has not reframed it.

**Where the story is poorer than the numbers justify:** capital allocation. Management barely discusses the buyback on these calls, yet in the June 2026 quarter alone the company repurchased $338.2 million of stock — about 3.3 million shares at roughly $102 each — and disclosed approximately $4.7 billion of remaining authorisation. Against a $13.8 billion market value, that authorisation is about a third of the company. At the June-quarter pace the share count shrinks roughly 9-10% a year, entirely funded from cash flow. It is the most valuable thing happening at Deckers that nobody on these calls talks about.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable, with a late-window shift from expansive to precise.**

- *May 2025 — peak confidence, offensive.* "another exceptional year," "incredible progress," a five-year scorecard recited in full. Guidance withheld for the full year, explicitly because of trade policy.
- *July 2025 — confident but hedged.* "off to a solid start." Fasching answers a direct question about store-versus-online comparable sales with "I don't know, Sam, that we want to go kind of down a path of breaking out that level of detail" — the first clear refusal in the window.
- *October 2025 — most defensive point.* The language turns to mitigation, promotion assumptions and levers. Fasching: "We don't have the same levers necessarily going into the back half." A rare forward warning: pressure "will continue into FY '27."
- *January 2026 — confidence restored, and earned.* "outstanding," "exceptional," and the clean line: "we've been cautious about the economy and the consumer, but never about our brands." Notably, this confidence arrived *with* the numbers, not ahead of them.
- *May 2026 — measured and specific.* "deep conviction in the durability of our model." Management introduces a multi-year framework (HOKA growing low double digits from fiscal 2028 through 2030) — the first time in the window it commits to numbers beyond one year. Committing to a three-year frame while guiding a down-margin year is a confident act.
- *July 2026 — the tone is not in the transcript set, but the disclosure is.* Full-year revenue and earnings guidance both raised, while the assumed tariff rate was lifted from 10% to 12.5%.

Guidance has become steadily *more* specific over the window, not less — the classic direction of travel for a management team that believes its own forecast. There is no shift into efficiency-and-cost language; investment language has if anything intensified.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High.**

Every one of the last twelve reported quarters beat the consensus earnings estimate. The pattern is systematic enough to be a policy rather than luck, and management effectively admits it — Fasching in July 2025: "Our assumption always embeds a level of more normalized promotion, and then we'll see how things play out. And if they play out like Q1, we may see some upside."

Tracking guidance given against results later delivered:

- HOKA was guided to low-teens growth for fiscal 2026 (cut from mid-teens once tariffs landed, October 2025). It delivered 16%. **Over-delivered.**
- The back half of fiscal 2026 was guided to low-20s operating margin with tariff pressure. The full year came in "above 23%." **Over-delivered.**
- Fiscal 2027 was pre-warned in October 2025 to carry first-half margin pressure. The company has since guided the full year to operating margin "slightly better than 21.5%" and earnings per share of $7.35 to $7.50, against $7.02 delivered. **Consistent with the warning, and raised once already.**

**The important qualifier, and it is a real one.** The *size* of the beat is compressing fast. Against consensus: the June 2025 quarter beat by about 36%, September 2025 by 15%, December 2025 by 20%, March 2026 by 18%, and the June 2026 quarter by only 6.8%. The sandbag cushion has thinned to roughly a fifth of what it was a year ago. Either expectations have finally caught up with the company's conservatism, or the conservatism has run out. Either way, the "they always beat big" reflex is now a weaker plank than it was.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The deflection that recurs most.** Analysts repeatedly ask for regional and channel detail and are repeatedly refused. Sam Poser of Williams Trading pushes three separate times across two calls for store versus e-commerce comparable sales and gets "clearly, the comp in our retail store was better than what we saw online, and we haven't broken that out" (July 2025). His frustration is explicit: "Can you please give us something here? I really think it's important." Management's answer never gets more specific than "retail performed better than e-commerce significantly." This is a genuine disclosure gap, though the underlying figure appears to be favourable rather than hidden bad news.

**The question that later turned into the news.** Jonathan Komp of Baird, October 2025, asked whether the back-half margin pressure was "more temporary" or "a permanent step down in the margin that you're willing to give up." Fasching's answer at the time pinned it on tariffs and promotion. Nine months later, fiscal 2027 operating margin is guided to about 21.5% against 23.6% two years earlier, and the *gross* margin has recovered while operating expenses have taken over as the drag. Komp asked the right question and did not get the right answer — the step-down has proved durable, and its cause has changed.

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing.** Two things. First, nobody has been given a bridge explaining why operating expenses should grow at more than twice the rate of revenue, or when that inverts. Management describes the spending ("oversized investments in the brand and brand-building capabilities across the globe," July 2025) without ever quantifying the return or naming the year it normalises. Second, the deceleration itself: HOKA's growth has gone 24%, 16%, 7.7% across three successive periods, and while management answers questions about the *drivers*, it has not addressed whether the low-double-digit multi-year framework is achievable off that trajectory.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- *Operating expenses running at more than twice revenue growth (June 2026 quarter):* $419.9 million, up 12.7%, against 5.7% revenue growth, turning a gross-margin improvement into a two-point operating-margin decline and flat earnings per share. Unquantified and open-ended.
- *The earnings-beat cushion is compressing* (see section 4): from roughly 36% a year ago to 6.8% in the latest quarter.
- *HOKA growth decelerating hard:* 24% in fiscal 2025, 16% in fiscal 2026, 7.7% in the June 2026 quarter — against a stated multi-year plan of low-double-digit growth through fiscal 2030.
- *Insider selling:* on open-market transactions only, one purchase of 1,825 shares against fourteen sales totalling 17,396 shares. Not alarming in scale, but it is not the pattern of a team that thinks the stock is materially undervalued.
- *Disclosure resistance* on channel-level detail, sustained across multiple calls and multiple analysts (section 5).
- *Rising tariff assumption:* the fiscal 2027 plan now assumes 12.5%, raised from 10%, and the replacement US trade measure has not been finalised — so the assumption itself could still move in either direction.

**Green flags**

- *Gross margin rose to 56.4% from 55.8% while absorbing an import tax* (June 2026 quarter), with fiscal 2027 guided above the year just completed. This is the cleanest possible evidence that the brands can price.
- *Genuine net cash of $1.13 billion* at 30 June 2026, with no goodwill and no long-term borrowings — a rare balance sheet in branded consumer goods.
- *Buyback of $338.2 million in a single quarter* with roughly $4.7 billion still authorised, about a third of the company's market value.
- *Twelve consecutive earnings beats*, and full-year guidance raised in July 2026 *while* the assumed tariff rate went up.
- *US demand inflected positively* in the December 2025 quarter after two soft quarters, driven by a membership programme and a cleaner product transition (January 2026 call).
- *Tariff refunds are real and excluded from guidance:* roughly $120 million was paid under the emergency-powers regime (May 2026 call), and the fiscal 2027 outlook "does not assume the collection of refunds for tariffs previously paid."
- *Discontinuing rather than defending weak brands:* the Koolaburra phase-out (January 2026) explains the small "other" segment decline and shows portfolio discipline.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**A quiet but important vocabulary shift.** Through 2025 management described HOKA in terms of individual shoes — the Clifton, the Bondi. From the October 2025 call onward the unit of description becomes the "franchise family": "Our franchises function as scalable platforms representing families of products, rather than single styles" (May 2026). This is not marketing language; it is a direct response to the biggest structural risk in performance running, which is that a brand lives or dies on one silhouette's fashion cycle. Management is deliberately engineering away single-product dependence, and the Mafate family (peak-performance, trail, and lifestyle versions launched together) is the proof of concept.

**A learning admission that raises rather than lowers credibility.** Caroti, October 2025, unprompted: "we probably have masked a few too many big product launches in the first half of the year, and we didn't space them out enough. There are a few learnings from us... it was a learning year for us." Chief executives rarely volunteer execution errors. The corrective — separating the Clifton and Bondi launch cycles so they "will no longer overlap" from autumn 2026 — is specific and dated.

**Channel strategy reversal, explained rather than hidden.** Deckers spent years prioritising direct-to-consumer selling, then in 2025 leaned back into wholesale. Fasching was careful to pre-empt the obvious criticism: "this is not a change in our strategy. This is us taking advantage of the opportunity presented to us" (May 2025). The evidence supports him — the shift tracked an observed consumer move back toward physical stores, and it did cost direct-to-consumer comparable sales in the short run exactly as management said it would.

**What the tariff-refund handling reveals about the customer relationship.** Asked how the roughly $120 million refund would be treated, Fasching said: "we have partners who were cost sharing in that. So we want to make sure that we're taking care of them" (May 2026). Two readings: the refund is worth materially less to shareholders than the gross figure, and Deckers is protecting wholesale relationships it will need for the door expansion it has planned. Both are true, and the second is the more valuable signal.

**The unspoken constraint.** Management has never once discussed a dividend, and discusses the buyback only when asked. For a company generating roughly $1.18 billion of free cash flow a year with $1.6 billion sitting in cash and no debt, the near-silence on capital returns while quietly retiring 9-10% of the shares annually is the loudest thing in the file.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.**

This is not a company in decline, and it is not the company it was in 2024 either. Revenue growth has settled from roughly 16% to roughly 6-10%. Earnings per share growth has settled from 30% to a guided 5-7%. Returns on capital remain outstanding at 28.3%, the balance sheet carries real net cash, and the pricing power that underwrites the whole business is demonstrably intact — the gross margin went *up* through a tariff shock. What has changed is that the company is now spending its operating leverage rather than banking it.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the tariff, and not the demand environment. It is whether the fiscal 2027 operating margin of roughly 21.5% is a trough or a new plateau. Every valuation of this business turns on that one question, because at 21.5% the stock is modestly cheap and at 18% it is not cheap at all. The company is guiding gross margin *higher* while guiding operating margin *lower*, which means the answer sits entirely in a discretionary spending line that management has never bridged, never quantified a return on, and never given a normalisation date for. Ask for that bridge before sizing up. The tripwire that would settle it in the wrong direction is gross margin slipping below about 55% alongside rising promotional activity — that would mean the spending is defensive rather than offensive.

**Economic moat: WIDE, and holding.** The moat type is intangible-brand — two labels consumers ask for by name, in a category where that is the only durable advantage available. The evidence for width is not the returns alone but their composition: a 56%-plus gross margin *sustained through an import tax and price increases that customers absorbed without volume loss*, 28.3% return on invested capital, measured share gains in US road running, and rising unaided brand awareness in every region (US 60%, Europe 40%, China 30%). A brand without pricing power cannot do that. The operating-margin decline that looks like erosion is, on inspection, an import tax plus a deliberate marketing step-up sitting below an expanding gross margin — which is a spending choice, not a competitive defeat. The trend is therefore stable rather than widening or eroding; it would be widening if the spending were converting into operating leverage, and it is not yet.

**Secular threat: manageable.** No structural force is eating this business's terminal value. Deckers is a brand owner, so the shift of retail toward online and direct channels helps rather than hurts it — the company sells through both and is currently benefiting from consumers returning to physical stores. The genuine long-run risk is ordinary fashion-cycle risk, which is severe in footwear and has killed better-regarded franchises, but it is a cyclical and executional risk rather than a one-way structural decline. Trade policy is the live external variable, and it is a tax on margin, not a threat to the franchise.

**Is the cheapness a mispricing or a trap?** A mispricing, but a moderate one rather than a dramatic one. The market is applying a de-rated footwear multiple — the multiple it has correctly assigned to Nike and Crocs, businesses earning roughly a third of Deckers' operating margin — to a company still growing, still gaining share, sitting on net cash, and retiring a tenth of its shares every year. That is a real gap. But the gap is not enormous, the earnings base is close to its own historical margin peak, and the deceleration in HOKA is genuine. This is a good business at a fair-to-modestly-attractive price, not a wounded compounder at a distressed one.

interrogator_dossier:
# Deckers Brands (DECK) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Forensic review of six consecutive quarterly earnings calls, May 2025 through July 2026, cross-checked against the reported financials. Share price used throughout: $99.23 (New York listing, US dollars, 27 July 2026).*

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Deckers sells two footwear brands: UGG, the 45-year-old sheepskin-boot franchise that has become a year-round premium lifestyle label, and HOKA, the thick-soled running brand it bought in 2013 and has grown into a roughly $2.9 billion business. A handful of small brands (Teva, AHNU, and the now-discontinued Koolaburra) make up the remaining 2-3% of sales.

Across these six calls the story moves through three distinct phases, and the shift is unusually easy to date.

**Phase one — victory lap (May 2025).** The fiscal 2025 wrap-up is the most confident management has sounded in the entire window. Revenue grew 16% to just under $5 billion, gross margin expanded 230 basis points to 57.9%, operating margin rose 200 basis points to 23.6%, and earnings per share grew 30% to $6.33. Chief executive Stefano Caroti framed it against a five-year record: revenue compounding at 19% a year, HOKA adding about $1.9 billion of revenue, UGG adding $1 billion, and earnings per share compounding at 32%. The word that recurs is "exceptional."

**Phase two — the tariff siege (July 2025 through January 2026).** Almost immediately the frame narrows. On the May 2025 call Caroti already flagged "a significant amount of uncertainty introduced as a result of shifting US trade policy," and for the next three quarters the story becomes a two-track narrative: brands winning, margins under a policy tax. By October 2025, chief financial officer Steve Fasching is explicit that the back-half margin decline is "really being driven by the tariffs," and — importantly — that the pressure "will continue into FY '27." The HOKA growth plan was cut from mid-teens (set before tariffs) to low teens (with them). Management is careful, repeatedly, to separate the two: demand is not the problem, the import tax is.

**Phase three — the brands answer, then the cost line bites (January 2026 through July 2026).** The January 2026 quarter is the vindication. Record revenue of $1.96 billion, HOKA up 18%, US revenue inflecting positively after two soft quarters, record earnings per share of $3.33, and this line from Fasching: "the quarter demonstrates that we have more pricing power." Caroti's summary is the most quotable thing in the transcripts: "We've been cautious about the economy and the consumer, but never about our brands."

The most recent quarter (reported 23 July 2026, after the transcript set) is where the arc turns again — and this time the pressure is self-inflicted rather than imposed. Revenue crossed $1 billion in a June quarter for the first time, up 5.7%. Gross margin actually *rose*, to 56.4% from 55.8%. But operating expenses grew 12.7% against 5.7% revenue growth, and earnings per share came in at $0.94 versus $0.93 a year earlier — essentially flat. The growth driver that was quietly retired over this window is US demand; the one that replaced it is international, which grew 50% in the June 2025 quarter and 38% across the first half of fiscal 2026.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

Management's biggest claims, tested against what the numbers actually did.

| Management's claim | Where and when | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pricing power is real; price rises stick | "we haven't seen any material decline in performance for the products that we have raised price on" (Jul 2025); "we have more pricing power" (Jan 2026) | Gross margin held 56-58% straight through a tariff shock, and in the June 2026 quarter *rose* to 56.4% from 55.8%. Fiscal 2027 gross margin is guided "slightly better than 56.5%" — above the year just finished | **Supported.** This is the single best-evidenced claim in the file |
| The scarcity model protects margin | "we manage a scarcity model. When we run low, it's helping us maintain high levels of gross margin" (May 2025) | Inventory at 31 March 2026 was down low single digits year on year while revenue grew 10%; gross margin stayed above 56% | **Supported** |
| Margin pressure is tariffs, not the business | "the declines that we're reflecting are really being driven by the tariffs" (Oct 2025) | Only partly true now. In the June 2026 quarter gross margin *improved* 60 basis points, yet operating margin fell roughly 200 basis points to 15.2%. The entire decline came from operating expenses of $419.9 million, up 12.7%. That is a spending decision, not an import tax | **Diverges.** The narrative under-owns a deliberate cost step-up |
| International is the growth engine | Emphasised every quarter from Jul 2025 | International revenue +50% (Jun 2025 quarter), +38% (first half fiscal 2026), +15% (Dec 2025 quarter). HOKA brand awareness US 60%, Europe 40%, China 30% (May 2026) | **Supported**, though the growth rate is decelerating sharply quarter by quarter |
| HOKA is gaining share | "HOKA gained 2 points of market share in the overall US Road running category" (Oct 2025, citing Circana) | HOKA grew 24% (fiscal 2025), 16% (fiscal 2026), and 7.7% in the June 2026 quarter. Share gains are real; the growth rate has more than halved in two years | **Supported but decaying** |
| Returns and balance sheet strength | Referenced via "fortified balance sheet" (Jan 2026) | Return on invested capital 28.3%, return on equity 34.8%, and genuine net cash of $1.13 billion at 30 June 2026 (cash of $1.60 billion against total debt of $472 million including $399 million of capitalised leases). No goodwill on the balance sheet | **Supported, and understated by management** |

**Where the story is richer than the numbers justify:** the framing of margin pressure as externally imposed. Three consecutive calls trained investors to read margin decline as a tariff story. The June 2026 quarter shows the gross margin — the true measure of pricing power — going the *right* way while operating margin falls two full points on internal spending. That is a materially different problem, and management has not reframed it.

**Where the story is poorer than the numbers justify:** capital allocation. Management barely discusses the buyback on these calls, yet in the June 2026 quarter alone the company repurchased $338.2 million of stock — about 3.3 million shares at roughly $102 each — and disclosed approximately $4.7 billion of remaining authorisation. Against a $13.8 billion market value, that authorisation is about a third of the company. At the June-quarter pace the share count shrinks roughly 9-10% a year, entirely funded from cash flow. It is the most valuable thing happening at Deckers that nobody on these calls talks about.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable, with a late-window shift from expansive to precise.**

- *May 2025 — peak confidence, offensive.* "another exceptional year," "incredible progress," a five-year scorecard recited in full. Guidance withheld for the full year, explicitly because of trade policy.
- *July 2025 — confident but hedged.* "off to a solid start." Fasching answers a direct question about store-versus-online comparable sales with "I don't know, Sam, that we want to go kind of down a path of breaking out that level of detail" — the first clear refusal in the window.
- *October 2025 — most defensive point.* The language turns to mitigation, promotion assumptions and levers. Fasching: "We don't have the same levers necessarily going into the back half." A rare forward warning: pressure "will continue into FY '27."
- *January 2026 — confidence restored, and earned.* "outstanding," "exceptional," and the clean line: "we've been cautious about the economy and the consumer, but never about our brands." Notably, this confidence arrived *with* the numbers, not ahead of them.
- *May 2026 — measured and specific.* "deep conviction in the durability of our model." Management introduces a multi-year framework (HOKA growing low double digits from fiscal 2028 through 2030) — the first time in the window it commits to numbers beyond one year. Committing to a three-year frame while guiding a down-margin year is a confident act.
- *July 2026 — the tone is not in the transcript set, but the disclosure is.* Full-year revenue and earnings guidance both raised, while the assumed tariff rate was lifted from 10% to 12.5%.

Guidance has become steadily *more* specific over the window, not less — the classic direction of travel for a management team that believes its own forecast. There is no shift into efficiency-and-cost language; investment language has if anything intensified.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High.**

Every one of the last twelve reported quarters beat the consensus earnings estimate. The pattern is systematic enough to be a policy rather than luck, and management effectively admits it — Fasching in July 2025: "Our assumption always embeds a level of more normalized promotion, and then we'll see how things play out. And if they play out like Q1, we may see some upside."

Tracking guidance given against results later delivered:

- HOKA was guided to low-teens growth for fiscal 2026 (cut from mid-teens once tariffs landed, October 2025). It delivered 16%. **Over-delivered.**
- The back half of fiscal 2026 was guided to low-20s operating margin with tariff pressure. The full year came in "above 23%." **Over-delivered.**
- Fiscal 2027 was pre-warned in October 2025 to carry first-half margin pressure. The company has since guided the full year to operating margin "slightly better than 21.5%" and earnings per share of $7.35 to $7.50, against $7.02 delivered. **Consistent with the warning, and raised once already.**

**The important qualifier, and it is a real one.** The *size* of the beat is compressing fast. Against consensus: the June 2025 quarter beat by about 36%, September 2025 by 15%, December 2025 by 20%, March 2026 by 18%, and the June 2026 quarter by only 6.8%. The sandbag cushion has thinned to roughly a fifth of what it was a year ago. Either expectations have finally caught up with the company's conservatism, or the conservatism has run out. Either way, the "they always beat big" reflex is now a weaker plank than it was.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The deflection that recurs most.** Analysts repeatedly ask for regional and channel detail and are repeatedly refused. Sam Poser of Williams Trading pushes three separate times across two calls for store versus e-commerce comparable sales and gets "clearly, the comp in our retail store was better than what we saw online, and we haven't broken that out" (July 2025). His frustration is explicit: "Can you please give us something here? I really think it's important." Management's answer never gets more specific than "retail performed better than e-commerce significantly." This is a genuine disclosure gap, though the underlying figure appears to be favourable rather than hidden bad news.

**The question that later turned into the news.** Jonathan Komp of Baird, October 2025, asked whether the back-half margin pressure was "more temporary" or "a permanent step down in the margin that you're willing to give up." Fasching's answer at the time pinned it on tariffs and promotion. Nine months later, fiscal 2027 operating margin is guided to about 21.5% against 23.6% two years earlier, and the *gross* margin has recovered while operating expenses have taken over as the drag. Komp asked the right question and did not get the right answer — the step-down has proved durable, and its cause has changed.

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing.** Two things. First, nobody has been given a bridge explaining why operating expenses should grow at more than twice the rate of revenue, or when that inverts. Management describes the spending ("oversized investments in the brand and brand-building capabilities across the globe," July 2025) without ever quantifying the return or naming the year it normalises. Second, the deceleration itself: HOKA's growth has gone 24%, 16%, 7.7% across three successive periods, and while management answers questions about the *drivers*, it has not addressed whether the low-double-digit multi-year framework is achievable off that trajectory.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- *Operating expenses running at more than twice revenue growth (June 2026 quarter):* $419.9 million, up 12.7%, against 5.7% revenue growth, turning a gross-margin improvement into a two-point operating-margin decline and flat earnings per share. Unquantified and open-ended.
- *The earnings-beat cushion is compressing* (see section 4): from roughly 36% a year ago to 6.8% in the latest quarter.
- *HOKA growth decelerating hard:* 24% in fiscal 2025, 16% in fiscal 2026, 7.7% in the June 2026 quarter — against a stated multi-year plan of low-double-digit growth through fiscal 2030.
- *Insider selling:* on open-market transactions only, one purchase of 1,825 shares against fourteen sales totalling 17,396 shares. Not alarming in scale, but it is not the pattern of a team that thinks the stock is materially undervalued.
- *Disclosure resistance* on channel-level detail, sustained across multiple calls and multiple analysts (section 5).
- *Rising tariff assumption:* the fiscal 2027 plan now assumes 12.5%, raised from 10%, and the replacement US trade measure has not been finalised — so the assumption itself could still move in either direction.

**Green flags**

- *Gross margin rose to 56.4% from 55.8% while absorbing an import tax* (June 2026 quarter), with fiscal 2027 guided above the year just completed. This is the cleanest possible evidence that the brands can price.
- *Genuine net cash of $1.13 billion* at 30 June 2026, with no goodwill and no long-term borrowings — a rare balance sheet in branded consumer goods.
- *Buyback of $338.2 million in a single quarter* with roughly $4.7 billion still authorised, about a third of the company's market value.
- *Twelve consecutive earnings beats*, and full-year guidance raised in July 2026 *while* the assumed tariff rate went up.
- *US demand inflected positively* in the December 2025 quarter after two soft quarters, driven by a membership programme and a cleaner product transition (January 2026 call).
- *Tariff refunds are real and excluded from guidance:* roughly $120 million was paid under the emergency-powers regime (May 2026 call), and the fiscal 2027 outlook "does not assume the collection of refunds for tariffs previously paid."
- *Discontinuing rather than defending weak brands:* the Koolaburra phase-out (January 2026) explains the small "other" segment decline and shows portfolio discipline.

## 7. Hidden signals

**A quiet but important vocabulary shift.** Through 2025 management described HOKA in terms of individual shoes — the Clifton, the Bondi. From the October 2025 call onward the unit of description becomes the "franchise family": "Our franchises function as scalable platforms representing families of products, rather than single styles" (May 2026). This is not marketing language; it is a direct response to the biggest structural risk in performance running, which is that a brand lives or dies on one silhouette's fashion cycle. Management is deliberately engineering away single-product dependence, and the Mafate family (peak-performance, trail, and lifestyle versions launched together) is the proof of concept.

**A learning admission that raises rather than lowers credibility.** Caroti, October 2025, unprompted: "we probably have masked a few too many big product launches in the first half of the year, and we didn't space them out enough. There are a few learnings from us... it was a learning year for us." Chief executives rarely volunteer execution errors. The corrective — separating the Clifton and Bondi launch cycles so they "will no longer overlap" from autumn 2026 — is specific and dated.

**Channel strategy reversal, explained rather than hidden.** Deckers spent years prioritising direct-to-consumer selling, then in 2025 leaned back into wholesale. Fasching was careful to pre-empt the obvious criticism: "this is not a change in our strategy. This is us taking advantage of the opportunity presented to us" (May 2025). The evidence supports him — the shift tracked an observed consumer move back toward physical stores, and it did cost direct-to-consumer comparable sales in the short run exactly as management said it would.

**What the tariff-refund handling reveals about the customer relationship.** Asked how the roughly $120 million refund would be treated, Fasching said: "we have partners who were cost sharing in that. So we want to make sure that we're taking care of them" (May 2026). Two readings: the refund is worth materially less to shareholders than the gross figure, and Deckers is protecting wholesale relationships it will need for the door expansion it has planned. Both are true, and the second is the more valuable signal.

**The unspoken constraint.** Management has never once discussed a dividend, and discusses the buyback only when asked. For a company generating roughly $1.18 billion of free cash flow a year with $1.6 billion sitting in cash and no debt, the near-silence on capital returns while quietly retiring 9-10% of the shares annually is the loudest thing in the file.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.**

This is not a company in decline, and it is not the company it was in 2024 either. Revenue growth has settled from roughly 16% to roughly 6-10%. Earnings per share growth has settled from 30% to a guided 5-7%. Returns on capital remain outstanding at 28.3%, the balance sheet carries real net cash, and the pricing power that underwrites the whole business is demonstrably intact — the gross margin went *up* through a tariff shock. What has changed is that the company is now spending its operating leverage rather than banking it.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the tariff, and not the demand environment. It is whether the fiscal 2027 operating margin of roughly 21.5% is a trough or a new plateau. Every valuation of this business turns on that one question, because at 21.5% the stock is modestly cheap and at 18% it is not cheap at all. The company is guiding gross margin *higher* while guiding operating margin *lower*, which means the answer sits entirely in a discretionary spending line that management has never bridged, never quantified a return on, and never given a normalisation date for. Ask for that bridge before sizing up. The tripwire that would settle it in the wrong direction is gross margin slipping below about 55% alongside rising promotional activity — that would mean the spending is defensive rather than offensive.

**Economic moat: WIDE, and holding.** The moat type is intangible-brand — two labels consumers ask for by name, in a category where that is the only durable advantage available. The evidence for width is not the returns alone but their composition: a 56%-plus gross margin *sustained through an import tax and price increases that customers absorbed without volume loss*, 28.3% return on invested capital, measured share gains in US road running, and rising unaided brand awareness in every region (US 60%, Europe 40%, China 30%). A brand without pricing power cannot do that. The operating-margin decline that looks like erosion is, on inspection, an import tax plus a deliberate marketing step-up sitting below an expanding gross margin — which is a spending choice, not a competitive defeat. The trend is therefore stable rather than widening or eroding; it would be widening if the spending were converting into operating leverage, and it is not yet.

**Secular threat: manageable.** No structural force is eating this business's terminal value. Deckers is a brand owner, so the shift of retail toward online and direct channels helps rather than hurts it — the company sells through both and is currently benefiting from consumers returning to physical stores. The genuine long-run risk is ordinary fashion-cycle risk, which is severe in footwear and has killed better-regarded franchises, but it is a cyclical and executional risk rather than a one-way structural decline. Trade policy is the live external variable, and it is a tax on margin, not a threat to the franchise.

**Is the cheapness a mispricing or a trap?** A mispricing, but a moderate one rather than a dramatic one. The market is applying a de-rated footwear multiple — the multiple it has correctly assigned to Nike and Crocs, businesses earning roughly a third of Deckers' operating margin — to a company still growing, still gaining share, sitting on net cash, and retiring a tenth of its shares every year. That is a real gap. But the gap is not enormous, the earnings base is close to its own historical margin peak, and the deceleration in HOKA is genuine. This is a good business at a fair-to-modestly-attractive price, not a wounded compounder at a distressed one.
